title: The Traveller and Fortune
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Traveller, exhausted with fatigue after a long journey, sank down at the very brink of a deep well and presently fell asleep. He was within an ace of falling in, when Dame Fortune appeared to him and touched him on the shoulder, cautioning him to move further away. "Wake up, good sir, I pray you," she said; "had you fallen into the well, the blame would have been thrown not on your own folly but on me, Fortune."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why did the Traveller sink down to rest?
options: He wanted to drink from the well
He was fleeing from a wild animal
He had injured his leg
He was exhausted with fatigue after a long journey

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where did the Traveller fall asleep?
options: At the very brink of a deep well
Under a large tree
Inside an abandoned house
On the road itself

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how close was the Traveller to falling into the well?
options: He was in no danger at all
He was within an ace of falling in
He had already fallen partway in
He was several yards away from the edge

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who appeared to warn the sleeping Traveller?
options: A passing shepherd
Another traveller
Dame Fortune
The well's owner

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "brink" mean in "the very brink of a deep well"?
options: The edge
The middle
The bottom
The roof

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "folly" mean in "not on your own folly"?
options: Wisdom
Good fortune
Foolishness or carelessness
Bravery

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does Fortune say that she, not the Traveller, would be blamed if he fell in?
options: Fortune had promised to protect all sleeping travellers
People often unfairly attribute misfortunes caused by their own carelessness to bad luck
Fortune was the one who dug the well
The Traveller had asked Fortune to watch over him

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Travellers should never rest near a well
Dame Fortune always protects those who are careless
Falling asleep outdoors is always dangerous
People tend to blame luck for troubles that are really caused by their own carelessness

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what are Fortune's exact opening words to the Traveller?
options: "Get away from that well at once!"
"You foolish man, look what you have done!"
"Wake up, good sir, I pray you"
"Do not sleep so close to danger"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did Fortune caution the Traveller to do?
options: Continue his journey immediately
Drink from the well before leaving
Wait until morning to travel
Move further away

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does the phrase "within an ace of" mean in "within an ace of falling in"?
options: Very close to
Far from
Certain to avoid
Unaware of

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "cautioning" mean in "cautioning him to move further away"?
options: Punishing
Congratulating
Ignoring
Warning or advising

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does Fortune's concern about being blamed suggest about her motive for waking the Traveller?
options: She acts purely out of love for the Traveller with no thought for herself
She is partly motivated by protecting her own reputation from unfair blame
She wants the Traveller to reward her later
She is required by law to wake sleeping travellers

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Traveller falls into a well and blames Dame Fortune
Dame Fortune pushes a sleeping Traveller into a well
A Traveller falls asleep near a well and Dame Fortune wakes him, pointing out that his own carelessness, not her, would be blamed if he fell in
A Traveller and Dame Fortune argue over directions
